bib.title: Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter 1: Introduction

question: What is reinforcement learning, how does it differ from supervised, unsupervised and evolutionary approaches, and what are its elements?
contributions: Defines RL as learning to map situations to actions to maximise a numerical reward, via trial-and-error search and delayed reward
Names four elements: policy, reward signal, value function, optional model
Tic-tac-toe worked example contrasting value-function TD learning with evolutionary search and minimax/DP
Early history in three threads: trial and error, optimal control, temporal difference

results.claim: Tic-tac-toe value table: terminal states with three Xs get value 1; three Os or full board get 0.
results.setup: Tic-tac-toe, RL player plays X; one table entry per board state, value = estimated P(win)
results.quote: Assuming we always play Xs, then for all states with three Xs in a row the probability of winning is 1

results.claim: All other tic-tac-toe states are initialised to 0.5, a 50% guess of winning.
results.quote: We set the initial values of all the other states to 0.5, representing a guess that we have a 50% chance of winning.

results.claim: TD update: V(St) <- V(St) + alpha[V(St+1) - V(St)], applied after greedy moves only; exploratory moves cause no learning.
results.setup: Tic-tac-toe vs a fixed imperfect opponent; backup from state after greedy move to state before it
results.quote: is a small positive fraction called the step-size parameter

results.claim: With step-size reduced properly over time the tic-tac-toe method converges to the true win probabilities and an optimal policy against that fixed opponent.
results.setup: Fixed opponent, step-size annealed; asserted not measured
results.quote: then this method converges, for any

results.claim: Backgammon has approximately 10^20 states, too many to visit; Tesauro combined the TD method with a neural network to generalise.
results.setup: TD-Gammon, Tesauro 1992, 1995 (text prints 1020, a superscript lost in extraction)

results.claim: RL has two distinguishing features: trial-and-error search and delayed reward.
results.quote: characteristics—trial-and-error search and delayed reward—are the two most important

limits: Book does not address constructing or learning the state signal (only briefly Sec 17.3)
Evolutionary methods are excluded from coverage by choice
Tic-tac-toe is stated to be so simple it may give the impression RL is more limited than it is; no experiments or measured results are reported
Convergence claim is asserted without proof in this chapter
practices: Keep the problem (RL), the solution methods and the field conceptually separate (Sec 1.1, p.2)
Treat draws and losses as equally bad in the tic-tac-toe setup; act greedily most of the time and occasionally explore (Sec 1.5, p.9)
Learn only from greedy moves in the example; exploratory moves cause no update (Fig 1.1)
Reduce step-size over time for convergence against a fixed opponent; keep it nonzero to track slowly changing opponents (p.10)

terms.definition: learning what to do—how to map situations to actions—so as to maximize a numerical reward signal
a mapping from perceived states of the environment to actions to be taken when in those states
a single number sent by the environment each time step; the agent's sole objective is to maximize total reward over the long run
the value of a state is the total amount of reward an agent can expect to accumulate over the future, starting from that state
something that mimics the behavior of the environment; given a state and action, predicts next state and next reward; used for planning
explicitly trial-and-error learners, viewed as almost the opposite of planning
agent must exploit what it has experienced to obtain reward but explore to make better action selections in future
apply multiple static policies, each interacting with a separate environment instance; best policies and random variations carry to the next generation; never estimate value functions
update driven by the difference V(St+1)-V(St) between estimates at two successive times
How do you distribute credit for success among the many decisions that may have been involved in producing it?
